entries.title: Russia: Putin party retains majority in controlled parliamentary vote
entries.summary: Vladimir Putin's United Russia won just under 58% of the vote, the electoral commission said. Meanwhile, Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov won nearly 100% of the vote in elections in the Russian republic of Chechnya.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russia: Putin party retains majority in parliamentary vote

September 21, 2026

Vladimir Putin's United Russia won just under 58% of the vote, the electoral commission said. Meanwhile, Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov won nearly 100% of the vote in elections in the Russian republic of Chechnya.

Russia's electoral commission on Monday said that the ruling United Russia party has won the parliamentary election.

It's the first parliamentary poll since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and President Vladimir Putin has cast it as a referendum of support for what is termed in Russia, the "special military operation."

Parties that support Putin and the Kremlin's war in Ukraine are the only ones registered to run, and the opposition was barred from taking part.

The polls took place amid rising prices, a crackdown on political opponents and the internet, fuel shortages and rumors of another mobilization drive following the elections.

What do we know about the Russian election results?

The Central Election Commission said that with 95% of ballots counted, the party of Russian President Vladimir Putin won 57.83% of the vote.

Commission chair Ella Pamfilova said that according to the preliminary results, United Russia would get 355 seats in the 450-seat Duma, giving the party around 20 more seats than it currently holds and marking the strongest result in its history.

The parliamentary vote was also the first to include residents of four regions in Ukraine — those being Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia —  that were occupied and illegally annexed by Moscow later that year.

Voting was also held in Crimea, which was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Kyiv denounced the voting in those regions as illegal.

Chechen ally receives nearly 100% of vote

Russia's electoral commission also announced that close Putin ally, Ramzan ​Kadyrov, has been re-elected to a fifth term as leader of Chechnya, a Russian republic in the North Caucasus region.

Electoral officials said he achieved 99.85% of the vote, a slight improvement from the 99.73% garnered in 2021.

International observers have previously severely criticised electoral processes in the small region.

Kadyrov's government has been accused of widespread rights violations by human rights organizations, including targeting journalists and homosexuals, something he denies.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Germany news: Trial starts of ex-Transport Minister Scheuer
entries.summary: Former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer is being tried for perjury related to a failed car toll scheme. And cherry farmers have brought in a bumper harvest. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Trial starts of ex-Transport Minister Scheuer

Published September 21, 2026last updated September 21, 2026

Former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer is being tried for perjury related to a failed car toll scheme. And cherry farmers have brought in a bumper harvest. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer stands accused of making false statements in connection with a failed scheme to charge foreign motorists highway tolls
  • Germany has had one of the best cherry harvests in years
  • Ever more people in Germany are using buses and trains for short trips, according to the Federal Statistical Office
  • German car exports sank considerably in the first seven months of the year, new figures show
  • Chancellor Friedrich Merz is under growing pressure after his CDU was badly defeated in two state elections

Here is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on September 21, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Automotive workers protest nationwide as industry suffers crisis

Automotive workers protest nationwide as industry suffers crisis

Protesters from Germany's automotive industry have called for action from the government and company managements to save their jobs and factories as the country's car production sector faces a growing crisis.

Tens of thousands of people are expected to take part in rallies, which, according to the IG Metall union — Europe and Germany's largest — will take place at more than 280 sites.

Car industry being driven 'into a brick wall'

Speaking at carmaker Volkswagen's Wolfsburg factory, IG Metall's chairwoman, Christiane Benner, who is also a member of  VW's supervisory board, said: "Things have really hit the fan."

"Companies like VW, BMW, Audi, Bosch, Mercedes and Porsche were synonymous with fantastic cars and high quality," she said.

"Now, management is driving the industry at full throttle into a brick wall."

Benner called on the government to bring down energy costs, give financial help to suppliers to help them adjust to new challenges and use "Made in EU" rules to bolster domestic production.

Massive job cuts underway

Many observers put the blame for the current crisis on companies having started too late with the shift to electric vehicles, while others say China's government support for its own producers has led to an unequal playing field in the sector.

US tariffs have also done their bit to damage what is one of Germany's key industries, while domestic demand has weakened.

VW itself plans to cut 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade in what would be the biggest ever restructuring in global automotive history, while Mercedes-Benz and BMW are also reducing their workforces.

Skip next section German car exports down in first seven months of 2026 — Destatis

German car exports down in first seven months of 2026 — Destatis

In 2026, German exports of passenger cars dropped by 4% up to the end of July in comparison with the same period last year, new figures by the Federal Statistical Office showed on Monday.

It exported altogether some 2 million cars at a worth of €73.5 billion ($84.4 billion), 8.9% less than a year ago, with almost a third going to the UK, the US and Italy.

Cars with electric and combustion engines both saw an export drop of 2.9%, while the export of those with hybrid motors fell by 8.2%.

Imports of new passenger cars rose by 16% to some 1.3 million vehicles.

China takes first place for car imports

Chinese vehicles climbed to first place among car imports to Germany at 175,000 vehicles.

That made up 13.8% of all car imports and represents a rise of 120.9% compared with the January-July period in 2025.

It thus pushed the former import leaders Czech Republic and Spain to second and third place respectively.

The rise in Chinese imports was largely driven by hybrid vehicles (+36%) and purely electric vehicles (+66%), while imports of Chinese cars with combustion engines went down 9%.

Skip next section Elections latest: Merz defiant after state poll drubbings

Elections latest: Merz defiant after state poll drubbings

Friedrich Merz's position as chancellor is looking increasingly fragile after his Christian Democrats (CDU) failed to make it into the state parliament of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in weekend elections.

And that result came on the heels of the election in Saxony-Anhalt around two weeks ago, in which the CDU also put in a poor showing amid big gains by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

That, combined with his already very low approval ratings, means Merz is currently under huge pressure.

DW looks at his predicament and the broader fallout from the recent polls in this dedicated blog: Germany: Friedrich Merz fights for survival after election defeats

Skip next section Germany brings in bumper cherry harvest

Germany brings in bumper cherry harvest

German orchard growers have harvested some 48,500 metric tons (53,462 US tons) of sweet and sour cherries this summer — 7.8% above the average for the past 10 years — new statistics show.

According to the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), some 80.2% of the harvest (38,900 tons) was sweet cherries, and 19.8% (9,600) was of the sour variety.

Pear growers also have reason to be content, with preliminary estimates putting the harvest of that fruit at 7.7% higher than the average over the past 10 years, though 3.3% down on last year.

The good fruit harvest comes despite Germany's grain production suffering greatly under the hot conditions during the summer.

Skip next section Ex-Transport Minister Scheuer goes on trial for perjury

Ex-Transport Minister Scheuer goes on trial for perjury

A perjury trial against former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer kicked off at the Berlin District Court on Monday.

Scheuer and his co-defendant Gerhard Schulz, a former state secretary, are accused of having lied to a parliamentary committee investigating a failed scheme some seven years ago to levy a highway toll on foreign motorists.

Both of them deny the charges made against them.

What are the charges against Scheuer and Schulz?

The two are accused of lying to the committee about having signed a contract with a company to run the toll operations despite knowing that the European Court of Justice (ICJ) was likely to declare the scheme illegal.

Scheur's Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of the Christian Democrats (CDU) currently led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz,  had devised a plan to levy tolls on all drivers but then compensate German motorists by reducing their motor vehicle taxes.

The scheme was shot down in 2019 by the ICJ for breaching EU rules.

But by that time, the Transport Ministry under Scheuer had already signed binding contracts with the operators who were to be tasked with executing the plan.

The German government was then forced to pay €243 million ($283 million at current exchange rates) in damages to the companies involved.

Jail sentences possible

The trial is planned to take place over 12 days, with a verdict expected on November 25.

If found guilty, the accused could face jail sentences ranging from three months to five years.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn wishes all its readers guten Tag at the start of a new week.

Among the big topics of the day in Germany is the start of a trial against former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer in connection with a failed car toll scheme that cost the government hundreds of millions of euros some seven years ago.

He stands accused of making false statements before a parliamentary committee investigating the issue.

In more positive news, cherry (and pear) farmers have something to smile about this year: They have had their best harvest in years owing to some mild spring weather.

And we will also, of course, be looking at the fallout from recent state elections that have brought bad news for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

Read on to find out more about these and other stories.

entries.title: Taliban says three killed in new Pakistan airstrikes on Afghanistan
entries.summary: The Afghan border provinces of Kunar and Paktika were reportedly struck. Pakistan last carried out deadly strikes on Afghanistan in June.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan airstrikes on Afghanistan kill 3, Taliban says

September 21, 2026

The Afghan border provinces of Kunar and Paktika were reportedly struck. Pakistan last carried out deadly strikes on Afghanistan in June.

Pakistan conducted airstrikes on northeastern Afghanistan on Monday on what Pakistani security officials described as militant hideouts, resulting in some deaths.

The two neighbors reported conflicting casualty tolls.

The Taliban government in Kabul claimed that three people were killed as it accused Pakistan of bombarding "civilian homes," while the Associated Press news agency cited two unnamed Pakistani security officials as saying that 28 suspected militants were killed.

Afghanistan's deputy government spokesperson Hamdullah Fitrat said that the strikes took place in the Kunar and Paktika provinces.

Fitrat wrote on X that one strike hit at around 3:00 am Monday (2230 UTC, Sunday) in Kunar's Nurgal district and "completely destroyed" a house, adding that three people were killed and four other members of the family were wounded.

He said that two locations were also hit in the Paktika province, claiming that a shop and an unoccupied house were destroyed.

There has yet to be an official statement from Pakistan on the strikes.

Strikes follow last week's militant attack in Pakistan

The reported strikes come after a suicide bombing and a 20-hour gun battle between militants and police on Friday, which took place at a district police headquarters compound in the Pakistani city of Kohat, situated near the Afghan border.

At least 31 people, including 16 police officers, were killed in the attack.

Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a local militant group linked to the jihadist group Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack.

The Afghanistan-Pakistan conflict

Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have been tense since the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calm after former South Asian allies engaged in their worst clashes in years in February.

Pakistan declared that month that it was in an "open war” with Afghanistan, following a rise in militant attacks on civilians and security forces inside Pakistan.

Afghanistan launched retaliatory strikes after Pakistan carried out airstrikes inside Afghan territory and the cross-border fighting has since claimed the lives of hundreds of people.

Pakistan last mounted deadly airstrikes in Afghanistan in June.

Islamabad accuses Afghanistan of sheltering militant groups which launch attacks inside Pakistan's territory.

Main among these is the TTP, often referred to as the Pakistani Taliban and Baloch separatist groups from the border areas.

The Taliban has dismissed ​the allegations, saying that militancy in Pakistan is an internal problem.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Germany's car crisis: Can the 35-hour workweek survive?
entries.summary: German carmakers want employees to work 40 hours instead of the current 35 without extra pay, arguing it would improve competitiveness. Unions strongly oppose the proposal and view it as an attack on workers' rights.
entries.content:
September 21, 2026

German carmakers want employees to work 40 hours instead of the current 35 without extra pay, arguing it would improve competitiveness. Unions strongly oppose the proposal and view it as an attack on workers' rights.

Germany's famed automotive sector is facing a deep crisis, squeezed by high manufacturing costs, punitive US tariffs, intensifying competition from China and a difficult transition to electric vehicles.  

Industry heavyweights such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.

The branch is shedding jobs faster than any other industrial sector in the country.

Volkswagen, for instance, is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW announced it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.

Auto suppliers such as Bosch and ZF Friedrichshafen have also announced thousands of job reductions amid tough market conditions and global competition.

Germany's automotive industry is losing competitiveness as costs rise and production shifts abroad, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, director of the Center for Automotive Research (CAR) in the German city of Bochum.

"In 2018, the industry employed around 830,000 people. Currently, that number is below 700,000," he told DW. "We project that by around 2030, it will be 500,000."

Regaining competitiveness and securing jobs in the future will require an array of measures including lower production and energy costs, better logistics infrastructure and favorable tax conditions, he added.

Labor costs too high in Germany?

Auto industry executives agree that labor costs in Germany are too high compared to international rivals.

Labor costs in the country average $3,307 (€2,882) per vehicle, compared to $769 in Japan and $597 in China, according to a reportpublished by the consulting firm Oliver Wyman.

To trim labor costs, carmakers want employees in Germany to work 40 hours a week instead of the current 35 hours, without any increase in pay.

The 35-hour workweek has long been standard across much of Germany's automotive industry, having emerged from collective bargaining agreements negotiated in the 1980s and 1990s.

It reflects an era when Germany was highly competitive, said Dudenhöffer, adding: "That time is over."

Workers' unions, however, vehemently oppose longer working hours.

Christiane Benner, the head of the influential IG Metall trade union, said workers had already accepted wage cuts and other concessions worth several billion euros, yet were now being told that this was still not enough.

The union argues that German automakers are struggling with weak demand and underutilized factories, not a shortage of labor hours. "Not a single additional car will be sold just because the workforce works longer hours," the union announced.

IG Metall is holding demonstrations at more than 200 locations nationwide on September 21 to oppose job cuts and other measures affecting working conditions in the automotive sector.

Can longer working hours save jobs?

The union is "fighting for relics from 20 years ago, forgetting today's reality," Dudenhöffer said.

The expert estimated that if carmakers were to move from a 35-hour week to a 40-hour week, personnel costs would decrease by 13%.

"We wouldn't be taking money away from employees, but we would be creating conditions that would make jobs possible in Germany, in the automotive industry, in the future," he underlined.

Stefan Bratzel, head of the Center of Automotive Management (CAM) in Bergisch Gladbach, said the 35-hour week represents a key achievement for trade unions in their collective bargaining history, so "conflict is inevitable" between management and unions.

On the other hand, more working hours for the same pay would mathematically lower labor costs per hour, he added.

"Ultimately, this raises the question of how the burdens of the current transformation are to be distributed between companies and employees," said Bratzel.

How can Germany's auto industry recover?

Experts say improving labor costs at German production sites is necessary, but it alone will not solve the industry's deeper structural problems.

"Working five hours more per week alone will not win the technological race against China," said Bratzel.

He stressed that, to restore their competitive edge, German carmakers need to deliver attractive and affordable electric vehicles, invest heavily in software and AI, and improve the efficiency of their development and manufacturing processes.

"German manufacturers must be at least as innovative and high-performing in technological terms as they are expensive by international standards," said Bratzel.

At the same time, he explained, Germany requires competitive framework conditions regarding energy, taxes, bureaucracy and infrastructure.

Dudenhöffer echoed this view, saying that Germany must pursue difficult but necessary reforms.

"Germany can only be considered a viable option for its automotive industry and jobs if we regain our competitiveness," he said.

And for that, action is required on multiple fronts, including lowering labor and energy costs, adjusting taxes, and creating better logistics infrastructure, he added.

"But the coming years will be very tough," Dudenhöffer warned. "And they will become even tougher if we stick to the status quo and believe we can simply rest on the prosperity we enjoyed 20 years ago."

Edited by: Tim Rooks

entries.title: US proposes AI safety mechanism in talks with China
entries.summary: US Treasury chief Scott Bessent said there had been "successful" talks with China on trade and AI. The talks come amid growing fears that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.
entries.content:
United States of America

US proposes AI safety mechanism in talks with China

September 21, 2026

US Treasury chief Scott Bessent said there had been "successful" talks with China on trade and AI. The talks come amid growing fears that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

Top officials fro the United States and China have discussed a communication mechanism dealing with AI concerns between the two countries.

The talks on Sunday evening come ahead of a summit this week between US President Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping and amid growing fears that AI poses an existential threat to humanity.

The discussion with a team led by China's Vice Premier He Lifeng also involved top US trade official Jamieson Greer and took place at JPMorgan Chase's New York headquarters.

What did US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent say about the AI talks with China?

"We just had a very successful engagement with the Chinese on trade and AI," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters.

Bessent said the delegations spoke about a mechanism to communicate about AI issues, calling it the "US-China AI dialogue."

"The US has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries," Bessent said.

The US Treasury chief said that these notifications would be for potential "incidents" or an instance "that rises up to a national security level from AI," he said, adding that both sides have agreed to meet again.

"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent said at the conclusion of the talks.

What has been reported in China?

Chinese state news agency Xinhua described the talks as "candid, in-depth, and constructive" on Monday.

"The two sides engaged in... discussions on key economic and trade issues of mutual interest, such as implementing the consensus from previous consultations and promoting bilateral trade and investment," Xinhua reported in a brief readout.

Xinhua added that Chinese and US officials also held a dialogue on "issues related to AI", with no further details provided.

 

Concern over the threat posed by AI

In recent weeks, leading AI firms have warned of the threat posed by unbridled AI development and the pace at which these threats could become a reality.

They have begun working on creating a standards body they say would regulate the industry amid rising fears about its dangers.

Late in August, more than 100 companies, including AI giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Perplexity, signed an open letter calling for a global effort to strengthen AI-powered cybersecurity threats.

That came after it emerged that OpenAI models had gone rogue and had hacked into a digital repository of AI technology.

Anthropic conducted investigations to see if its own models had carried out similar attacks and found three incidents in which a Claude model and later identified a fourth incident.

AI experts sound the alarm

Earlier this month, researcher Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI employee, resigned from Anthropic, warning that AI companies were "gambling with our lives."

Former Google DeepMind researcher Bilal Chughtai echoed his concerns, warning that "AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome."

Trump has dismissed calls to better curb AI's development as "hoaxes" and a "conspiracy."

Trump's stance has been applauded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose chipmaking company powers the vast majority of AI systems. Huang thanked the US president for "seeing through" the warnings on AI.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: India news: India's medal tally at Asian games rises to six
entries.summary: Indian athletes won two bronze and two silver medals on the second day of the Asian Games in Japan. Meanwhile, more bodies were recovered after a flash flood in Kerala. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India's medal tally at Asian games rises to six

Published September 21, 2026last updated September 21, 2026

Indian athletes won two bronze and two silver medals on the second day of the Asian Games in Japan. Meanwhile, more bodies were recovered after a flash flood in Kerala. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • India ups medal tally on day 2 of Asian Games in Japan
  • At least five dead in Kerala after flash floods
  • Bihar police responds to viral video showing alleged molestation of minor

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Monday, September 21: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section India studying US tariff on Russian oil buyers, trade minister says

India studying US tariff on Russian oil buyers, trade minister says

The Indian government is studying the details of US tariffs on buyers of Russian oil, Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said on Monday.

Goyal's comments came days after Washington passed and sanctions and tariffs bill allowing US President Donald Trump to impose stiff tariffs of up to 100% on India, China and other countries which continue to depend on Russian energy.

India-US ties facing test

While India and Russia ties have grown stronger since the start of the war in Ukraine, driven largely by Russian oil exports, the same cannot be said of India-US relations under Prime Minister Narendra Modi as tensions mounted over New Delhi's purchases of Russian oil.

Last August, Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian imports over those purchases, on top of a 25% reciprocal tariff.

However, the additional Russia-related tariff was removed in February 2026, while the reciprocal tariff was reduced to 18% as part of a US-India trade framework.

That landmark bilateral trade agreement between the two countries remains in limbo, with no significant breakthrough and experts argue that Washington is likely to use the threat of additional tariffs as leverage for a favorable deal with India.

Skip next section India's premier tech institute apologizes after alleged student suicide

India's premier tech institute apologizes after alleged student suicide

The Indian Institute of Technology, one of the country's premier Institutes, issued an apology on Monday for its earlier communication regarding an alleged student suicide which has led to protests.

"The details and circumstances leading up to the incident remain subject to investigation by the appropriate authorities. In view of the ongoing investigation, it was inappropriate to have set out or characterized details..." the institute said in a post on X.

A student suicide and what followed

A second-year student of the Department of Energy Science and Engineering reportedly died on September 18. A day later, the institute issued a statement on social media saying the 20-year-old died by suicide after he was found using a mobile phone in the examination hall, allegedly attempting to seek answers from ChatGPT.

He was found dead in his room later that evening, it added.

Students at IIT Bombay have since staged protests demanding an investigation and action against the professor suprevising the exam. The deceased student's family had also reportedly named the same professor in the police investigation, alleging harassment and caste discrimination.

On September 20, IIT Bombay's Director, Professor Shireesh Kedare, met protesting students and later suspended the professor in question while he was being investigated, Indian media reported.

Skip next section Viral video shows group of men grabbing minor girl, police responds

Viral video shows group of men grabbing minor girl, police responds

Videos showing a group of men in the eastern state of Bihar harassing two minors, including a girl, were going viral on social media on Monday.

The initial video, seemingly shot at night, showed a group confronting a young man and woman, apparently because they were together alone. One of the perpetrators is seen grabbing the girl from the bottom, hoisting her in the air, to rush her away from her companion.

More videos of the incident surfaced later, showing the couple surrounded by a mob while they were visibly distressed. We are not including the video because of its sensitive nature.

Indians demand arrests

Enraged netizens reacted to the video, tagging local police and demanding accountability and arrests.

"The video from Jamui, Bihar is deeply disturbing," Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi wrote on social media. "Two Class 10 students were stopped on a road. Harassed. Humiliated. Molested. A young girl, hands folded, begged to be let go while goons groped her and dragged her away," he said.

"Every individual in that video must be identified and prosecuted under POCSO, and justice must be swift. And if the incident happened on September 19th, why are the culprits not behind bars yet?" he added. POCSO stands for the Protection of Children from Sexual Offenses Act.

How have police responded?

Local police confirmed that the two victims were minors who had gone to the location to take pictures, and that a criminal complaint (First Information Report or FIR) had been made. "The accused will be identified and arrests ensured at the earliest," Jamui Police said on social media.

Meanwhile, Jamui SP Vishwajeet Dayal said the video came to the department's attention on Monday morning.

"Based on the video, we identified the victims and recorded their statements. It came to light that the incident took place around 7 pm on September 19. The two friends, a boy and a girl, had gone for coaching and had gone to the area, where the incident occurred, to take photographs," the officer told reporters.

"The accused have been identified. We are taking legal action and the accused will be arrested soon," Dayal said.

Skip next section Delhi's VIPs under scanner amid electoral roll revision

Delhi's VIPs under scanner amid electoral roll revision

Delhi's revision of electoral rolls is in the spotlight once again, with several VIPs in government and politics receiving notices for "discrepancies" in their submitted voter Information.

That includes India's Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, India's Election Commissioner Sukhbir Singh Sandhu, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri and several former leaders, both from the Ruling Bharatiya Janata Party and the opposition, Indian media reported on Monday.

Delhi's Chief Minister Rekha Gupta also received a notice for an age discrepancy, the Times of India reported.

SIR, or the Special Intensive Revision, is an exercise conducted by the Election Commission of India (ECI) to remove redundancies in India's electoral rolls. The discrepancies arising from this process often include mismatches in names, family details or age, which can be rectified by providing a list of pre-approved documents to local officers. 

A controversial process

The SIR has been a controversial exercise over the last few years. The latest round of SIR was announced by the ECI in October 2025 and several states have undergone the process already.

Opposition leaders and critics have argued that those struck off in the exercise include a heavy proportion of minority voters and that Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP is using it as a tool to secure future electoral wins. 

The BJP has dismissed such claims, arguing that those removed largely involve dead voters and illegal infiltrators, thereby protecting India's democracy.

A recent report by The Reporter's Collective said about 54.6% of the capital's existing voters had either been struck off the voting list or had been served notices by the ECI, with the burden of proof falling on the voters.

Skip next section Kerala flash flood: Death toll rises, more rain expected

Kerala flash flood: Death toll rises, more rain expected

Search and rescue authorities in the southern state of Kerala found three more dead bodies on Monday morning, taking the death toll from a flash flood to at least five.

Six people were swept away on Sunday evening in the scenic town of Nilambur when the Kottapuzha River rose due to rainfall higher up in the landscape, local media reported. The search for the sixth person is still on.

Floods and rain-triggered landslides are a common occurrence in Kerala during the monsoon months, between June and November.

The state's Chief Minister VD Satheesan is set to arrive in the town shortly.

Meanwhile, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued orange alerts for six districts in the state on Monday morning, warning of more downpour.

An orange alert is the second highest in IMD's four-stage color-coded system, sitting just below the red warning. It tells local authorities and residents to 'be prepared' for heavy to very heavy rainfall in the region.

Skip next section Asian Games: India gains four more medal on day 2

Asian Games: India gains four more medal on day 2

Indian athletes picked up two silver and two bronze medals on the second day of the Asian Games 2026 in Japan, taking the nation's tally to six.

Historically, the Asian Games and the Commonwealth Games are where India gains most of its medals at an international level.

Indian shooters Himanshu Dhillon and former world champion Rudrankksh Patil secured India a two-podium finish in the men's 10-meter air rifle event on Monday, winning a silver and a bronze medal respectively.

These medals came barely an hour after they, along with Parth Mane, won a silver in the men's 10-meter air rifle team event for shooting an aggregate qualification score of 1890.1.

30-year-old Suchika Tariyal settled for a bronze in the women's traditional 60 kg mixed martial arts event on Monday after a close-call fight with Singapore's Hui Hoon Teo. Tariyal was seen weeping after the final decision went in Teo's favor on a post-draw technicality where the lighter athlete is awarded the win.

This takes India's overall tally to six medals after picking up two silver medals in the women's 10 meter air rifle competition on Sunday.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! and welcome to DW's India blog, where you will find the biggest headlines from the country.

This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from the New Delhi studio, where a slight nip in the air is reminding us that we're in the latter half of September.

Diving right into it, it's day two of the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya Japan and Indian athletes have cinched four more medals in shooting and mixed martial arts, taking India's total tally to six so far.

Coming to India, a flash flood in the southern state of Kerala has left at least five dead. India's weather agency has issued a heavy rainfall alert in six districts in the state for today.

Also in news is an ongoing boardroom battle at one of India's largest private conglomerates, Tata Sons, as the company hashes it out with its controlling charitable organization over the reappointment of its chairman and a possible public listing.

Stay tuned for all of this and more.

entries.title: Japan: Typhoon Dujuan sparks flood, landslide warnings
entries.summary: Evacuation advisories have been issued and hundreds of flights have been canceled in Japan, which is in the middle of a five-day holiday. The storm could dump record levels of rain on the country.
entries.content:
Japan

Japan: Typhoon Dujuan sparks flood, landslide warnings

September 21, 2026

Evacuation advisories have been issued and hundreds of flights have been canceled in Japan, which is in the middle of a five-day holiday. The storm could dump record levels of rain on the country.

A powerful typhoon was nearing Japan's eastern coast on Monday, triggering flood and landslide warnings, evacuation advisories and prompting hundreds of flights to be canceled.

The Japan Meteorological Agency issued level 5 emergency warning for the Izu islands, with the advisory cautioning a "life-threatening situation" and for residents to "ensure safety immediately."

A level 5 warning is the highest level of alert on the agency's scale.

Dujuan is forecast to pass close to the Tokyo metropolitan area later in the day and than one million people have been reported to be under evacuation advisories.

What do we know about Typhoon Dujuan?

Typhoon Dujuan was packing winds at speeds of 144 kilometers (89 miles) per hour as it lingered some 110 kilometres from Hachijojima, one of Tokyo's most remote islands.

Parts of the Izu Islands and the Chiba prefecture near Tokyo already saw heavy rainfall over the weekend.

The ⁠Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) has cautioned that weather conditions could worsen rapidly.

"The total rainfall through Tuesday could exceed the average monthly rainfall for September, resulting in record-breaking heavy rain," the JMA said.

Authorities have also warned of a possibility of ⁠linear ​rain bands forming over central Japan and the Kanto region — which includes Tokyo and surrounding prefectures — that could raise the risk of rain-related disasters like flash floods and landslides.

Linear ‌bands cause heavy torrential rainfall ​over a narrow area for several hours.

How have Japan's regions been affected by the incoming storm?

Over 4,000 households in Chiba were without power.

In the central prefecture of Aichi, which is currently hosting the Asian Games, an equestrian eventing competition was postponed until Tuesday.

The Tokyo Game Show, one of the world's biggest video game trade fairs, was shut down ahead of its final day on Monday.

Dujuan could also scupper travel plans during Japan's "Silver Week" holiday, which has just begun and which normally sees a surge in domestic travel.

On Monday, Japan Airlines canceled 120 domestic and 15 international flights, while All Nippon Airways canceled 140 domestic flights.

Some railway services were suspended on some lines in Tokyo and its neighboring areas.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: US: Man wounded in Texas after being shot by ICE agent
entries.summary: An ICE agent shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas. The city's mayor has called for an independent investigation into the shooting.
entries.content:
September 21, 2026

An ICE agent shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas. The city's mayor has called for an independent investigation into the shooting.

A man has been hospitalized in Austin, Texas after being shot by an officer of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), local officials said Sunday.

Austin's Mayor Kirk Watson expressed his anger over the shooting, calling for the involvement of the local police in a "clear-eyed" investigation into the incident.

What do we know about the ICE shooting in Austin?

The man suffered one gunshot wound in his torso during a brief foot pursuit in the Texan capital's north side shortly before 1 pm local time, Austin officials said at a press briefing.

He is at a local hospital in a serious but stable condition, the officials said, adding that the information on the incident was "very preliminary."

City police officers were not involved in the operation or the shooting, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said.

Who is the man wounded by ICE agent?

The officials did not name the man or release his age and nationality but an immigration lawyer, representing his family, identified him as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan.

Attorney Kate Lincoln Goldfinch said in a video published on her Instagram account that she believed he had no criminal history and had no final order to be removed from the country.

The Associated Press later cited Goldfinch as saying that she did not know his current immigration status.

There is yet to be a statement on the shooting from ICE or the Department of Homeland Security that oversees the immigration agency.

Meanwhile, a group of about 100 protesters gathered at the site of the shooting and demonstrated against ICE's actions.

The protest was held across the street from a blue Toyota Corolla which had damage to its ​passenger-side door, news agency Reuters reported citing local TV, as ICE agents stood nearby.

Austin Mayor rails against 'rogue' ICE, calls for independent probe

Sunday's shooting is the latest in a slew of incidents involving ICE, which has become the face of an immigration clampdown by US President Donald Trump's Republican administration.

Watson, a Democrat, told the media that the shooting occurred amid a "significant increase, almost overnight" of ICE operations in Austin.

"While I'm angry and disappointed, I'm not surprised. This has happened in other cities. With the rogue nature of ICE and the chaos we're seeing fomented by ICE, there's no reason to be surprised," the Austin mayor wrote on X.

He called for an independent investigation into the shooting, with the Austin Police Department (APD) having a role in the probe.

He said that the people of Austin had a "right to know what happened" and "a right to feel safe in their community".

"Though APD was not involved in the shooting, I believe that there needs to be an investigation that APD assures is clear-eyed, as complete as possible, and independent," Watson said.

He added that police chief Davis had deployed the APD's Special Investigation Unit at the scene, elaborating that the unit is the one responsible for probing Austin's officer-involved shootings.

Watson said that Davis has also asked the Texas Rangers to help out in the investigation.

'Horror has come to our doorstep,' says Congressman

On Sunday, US Representative Greg Casar — a Texas Democrat — called for transparency as the shooting is investigated.

He accused ICE of not being "truthful" in shooting in other cities.

"It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep," Casar said.

"A few weeks ago as we saw the ICE surge come ... I and others said that ICE needed to leave before someone was shot," he told the media.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Iran closes language center in Tehran, France vows response
entries.summary: In response to the Iranian authorities' decision to close a French language center affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, France vowed to take appropriate measures.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran closes language center in Tehran, France vows response

September 21, 2026

In response to the Iranian authorities' decision to close a French language center affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, France vowed to take appropriate measures.

Paris will summon Iran's ambassador and take appropriate measures in response after Iranian authorities closed a French language center affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, the French Foreign Ministry said on Sunday.

"This new attack against France's cultural presence in Iran, following the assault on two staff members of the French embassy last July, is unjustifiable and ​unacceptable," the ministry's spokesperson Pascal Confavreux said in a statement.

What do we know about the center's closure?

Earlier on Sunday, Iranian authorities announced the closure of a French language center in Tehran following a judicial order from the prosecutor's office.

"The illegal center affiliated with the French embassy in Tehran, which has operated for years under the guise of language instruction, was closed," the judiciary's Mizan news website said, referring to the French Language Center (CLF).

The Iranian judiciary accused the center of conducting "illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions".

It also accused the center of having "abused its status as a language training facility" and of having sought to "identify and build networks among the country's elite figures while facilitating their departure."

Tensions between Paris and Tehran

France has previously dismissed such allegations. The country claims that there has been a pattern of intimidation in recent months as it has sought to increase support for and contact with Iran's civil society following the crackdown on protests at the beginning of this year.

Tensions between Tehran and Paris have been escalating in recent years. Last month, France expelled two Iranian diplomats in response to the brief detention and prohibition of two French envoys to the Islamic Republic. Tehran accused the diplomats of interfering in its internal affairs.

Diplomats said Iran was also upset by a recent social media post from French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot commemorating the fourth anniversary of Mahsa Amini's death, which sparked protests nationwide.

In response, on Friday, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi called the post "crocodile tears" and accused Paris of slaughtering 1.5 million Algerians during Algeria's war of independence.

The two ministers are scheduled to meet on Tuesday at the United Nations' annual gathering of world leaders.

entries.title: Canada, France agree to closer ties in defense, economy
entries.summary: Amid strained relations with the US, French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced closer economic and defense ties.
entries.content:
Canada

Canada, France agree to closer ties in defense, economy

September 20, 2026

Amid strained relations with the US, French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced closer economic and defense ties.

French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced deeper cooperation between their countries in many areas, including defense, energy, and business.

The two leaders made the announcement on Sunday from Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a small French territory just off the Atlantic coast of Canada.

According to a statement from Carney's office, the leaders discussed aerospace, energy, critical minerals, and advanced technologies, such as quantum computing, satellites, and supercomputing.

This move is another step in Canada's accelerating turn toward Europe, as both countries are experiencing strained relations with the US.

The meeting between Macron and Carney follows up on Carney's visit to Brussels, during which the EU offered Canada "associate member" status.

What did the leaders say?

"We both believe that our countries are two great, independent nations who want to remain so," Macron said at the joint news conference, adding that France and Canada would work together for closer ties on fishing, security and energy.

"We both believe in democracy, the rule of law, respect for free and fair trade, the science on which our decisions are based, and the strategic autonomy that we defend," Macron said. "And this is what very deeply unites Canada and France, Canada and the European Union."

Meanwhile, Carney said: "The time has come to tighten our links between Canada and France, between Canada and the European Union — links based on the values we share."

"History remembers those who... defend their sovereignty, those who stay true to their values," Carney stressed in his speech.

However, he also proposed that France, Canada, the United States and China work together on artificial intelligence.

Where is Saint Pierre and Miquelon?

Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a French overseas territory, is located off the coast of Newfoundland and has a population of fewer than 6,000 people.

It is France's only remaining possession in North America and a remnant of its former vast territories in what are now Canada and the United States. One of Canada's provinces, Quebec, has French as its sole official language.

Macron's three-day visit to Saint Pierre and Miquelon is the first by a French president in over a decade. Carney is the first Canadian prime minister to visit the territory.

The leaders' meeting comes at a time of strained relations with the US. Ottawa has strongly rejected President Donald Trump's repeated remarks about making Canada the 51st US state.

Last Monday, Trump posted a map of North America on social media. The map depicted Canada, Greenland, Mexico, much of Central America and the Caribbean, and Iceland in the colors of the US flag.

Several French overseas territories were also included in the image, such as Guadeloupe, Martinique, and Saint Pierre and Miquelon.

However, upon his arrival in the territory late Saturday, Macron reaffirmed its status as French territory and dismissed "strange ideas" on the subject.
